title: Don't despair of mercy (Berakhot 10a)
hookLine: Hezekiah: even with a sword on your neck, don't give up on mercy
tomorrow: why would a king say the same line five times?

cards: The test results come back, and the doctor's face says it before the words do. Some people go quiet; some get very practical.
Berakhot tells of a king who got that kind of news from a prophet, and the first thing he did was talk back.

teach.b: Isaiah comes to King Hezekiah, who is sick, and says, in the Jewish Publication Society's words: "Set thy house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live."
The Talmud imagines Hezekiah's reply: son of Amoz, finish your prophecy and go.

teach.h: A SWORD ON THE NECK: STILL ASK.
teach.b: I have a teaching from my ancestor's house: even if a sharp sword rests on a person's neck, he should not hold himself back from asking for mercy.
Then, in the book of Isaiah, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays, and God answers that the prayer was heard, and adds years to his life. One question for today: when is it too late to hope?
The Talmud's answer: not while you can still ask. Here's the unity thread. The Qur'an says something close, in its own words.

teach.h: DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation, God tells those who have wronged themselves: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah." Two traditions, one refusal: mercy isn't closed while a person is still turning toward it.
And the honest difference. Hezekiah, facing death, asks for more life; his story is about danger. The Qur'an's verse speaks to people weighed down by what they've done; it's about forgiveness.
Same door, different rooms behind it.
One to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, a king tells a prophet to finish talking, because he still has a prayer to say.

how: Jews pray for people who are ill by name, often with the Mi Sheberach prayer in synagogue, and personal prayers for healing can be added to the daily Amidah.

games.q: what does “don't despair of mercy” mean?
o: never let other people see that you're afraid
even at the very edge, keep asking for mercy
mercy goes only to those who never lose hope

games.q: the king, the prophet, the neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: still, don't stop asking for mercy
despair not of the mercy of Allah

s: Hezekiah accepts the prophet's word and stops praying
he answers back: even with a sword on your neck, don't hold back from asking for mercy.
the Qur'an has the line 'Despair not of the mercy of Allah'
in Pickthall's translation, spoken to those who have wronged themselves.
Hezekiah's story and the Qur'an's verse are about exactly the same thing
same door, different rooms: Hezekiah asks for life in danger; the Qur'an's verse speaks of forgiveness.

games.q: a friend got turned down by every school she applied to and says there's no point asking for anything now. what does Hezekiah's line point to?
o: keep asking: an appeal, a waitlist, another door. it's not over while she can ask.
accept it quietly; a decision like that is final, like a prophet's word.
stop hoping for a while; asking again will only hurt her more.
games.why: Hezekiah heard 'you will die' from a prophet and still turned to the wall to pray. the Talmud's line: even with a sword on your neck, don't hold back from asking.

practice: Take a pen and write, by hand, one hard thing you're facing, in a single line. Underneath it, write one small thing you can still ask for inside it: help, time, a better day. Rest your eyes on that second line for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Don't despair of mercy. Hezekiah's teaching: even with a sword on your neck, keep asking.

orig.note: Hebrew: let him not hold himself back from mercy, Hezekiah's teaching in Berakhot 10a.

carryVoice: For the hard days: don't despair of mercy, not while you can still ask. Berakhot, day ten.
